Milacemide was initiated at 800 mg/day and was gradually increased to a maximum dosage of 2,400 mg/day. No significant improvement occurred in the 10 patients.

glycine is an inhibitory neurotransmitter in the cns (1). it causes membrane hyperpolarisation and inhibits neuronal firing (2). defective glycinergic systems may be important in animal models of spinal rigidity (3,4), and this has led to speculation that abnormalities of glyciner- gic inhibition by spinal interneurones may be important in the stiff-person syndrome (5). several animal studies have also suggested that defec- tive glycinergic systems may result in myoclonus. thus, the stereotactic infusion of the glycine receptor antago- nist, strychnine, into the medullary reticular formation induces generalised stimulus-sensitive myoclonus in the rat (6). in urea-induced myoclonus, urea has been shown to displace glycine at its receptor sites in the brainstem (7), and in ddt-induced myoclonus, intraventricular gly- cine is effective in suppressing the myoclonus (8). in poll hereford calves with inherited myoclonus, there is a spe- citic and marked deficit in strychnine binding sites in the spinal cord, reflecting a loss of, or defect in, glycine re- ceptors (9). milacemide is a glycine precursor that penetrates the blood-brain barrier effectively, before being converted into glycinamide and glycine (10). it is reasonably well tolerated (1 1). we report an open-label trial of milacemide in seven patients with myoclonus of various types, and three patients with the stiff-person syndrome. address correspondence and reprint requests to prof. c. d. marsden, university department of clinical neurology, insti- tute of neurology, queen square, london, wcln 3bg, en- gland. patients and methods ten patients were enrolled in the study (table 1). there were four patients (cases 14) with postanoxic multifocal action myoclonus. the action myoclonus was cortical in origin, and a cortical correlate in the backaveraged elec- troencephalographic activity preceded and was time- locked to the jerks occurring on action. somatosensory evoked potentials were normal in these four patients, and there was no evidence of stimulus-sensitive myoclonus. one patient (case 5) had myoclonic dystonia. the jerks markedly improved with alcohol. he was the product of a prolonged and difficult labour. there was no relevant family history. there was no electrophysiological evi- dence that the myoclonus in this patient was cortical in origin. one patient (case 6) had propriospinal myoclonus of unknown aetiology, and has been previously reported (12). another patient (case 7) had axial myoclonus and paroxysmal axial spasms, presumed to be propriospinal in origin, and has also been previously reported (p. brown et al., unpublished observations). the final three patients (cases 8, 9, and 10) had slowly progressive axial stiffness, with electrophysiological evidence of continu- ous muscle fibre activity at rest in paraspinal muscles. all three patients had serological evidence of autoimmune disease, one patient had a history of pernicious anaemia, and a second had a history of insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus. two of the three patients had anti-glutamic acid decarboxylase antibodies in the cerebrospinal fluid. the Title:
A therapeutic trial of milacemide in myoclonus and the stiff-person syndrome.

Metadata abstract:
We investigated the therapeutic effects of milacemide in seven patients with myoclonus and three patients with the stiff-person syndrome in an open-label trial. Milacemide was initiated at 800 mg/day and was gradually increased to a maximum dosage of 2,400 mg/day. No significant improvement occurred in the 10 patients.
